title: Mantle plume sources started dry, water was later introduced by subduction
dek: Noble gas isotope models show that the mantle plume source had 4 to 250 times less water than the upper mantle during Earth's accretion, but today exceeds the upper mantle by 20 times—supplied by subduction-zone water.
why: This episode thoroughly explains the niche method of noble gas isotopes, with an information-dense core insight—mantle plumes went from dry to wet—though the mid-section on isotope principles is technical.
who: Geology enthusiasts interested in deep-Earth water cycling, plate subduction, and mantle plume mechanisms, as well as people wanting to understand the noble gas isotope research method.
skip: 9:17–11:21 covers the mathematical principles of radiogenic/primordial isotope ratios in technical detail; you can skip to 11:21 to see the conclusions if the details are unclear.

points.h: Ocean ridge and plume basalts come from separate mantle reservoirs
points.body: Ocean ridge magma rises from shallow mantle during plate separation, while hotspot volcanoes like Hawaii and the Galápagos draw from deep mantle plumes confirmed by seismic imaging. Their chemical differences fall into two categories: internal variation in hotspot basalts far exceeds that in ocean ridge basalts; additionally, hotspot basalts retain signals from radioactive isotopes that became extinct within the first billion years of Earth's formation. This indicates that the two reservoirs remained separate throughout most of Earth's history, never fully mixed by convection.

points.h: Radiogenic-to-primordial isotope ratios measure how much mantle has degassed
points.body: Every noble gas has a ‘primordial isotope’ (inherited from primordial gases at Earth's accretion) and at least one ‘radiogenic isotope’ (continuously produced by decay of uranium, thorium, and similar radioactive elements). If a reservoir has degassed little and retained most of its primordial gas, the ratio of radiogenic to primordial isotopes becomes diluted and appears low; if it has degassed heavily, primordial gases escape while non-volatile parent elements like uranium and thorium remain in minerals, continuing to produce new gas through decay, making this ratio very high.

points.h: Helium, neon, and argon show mantle plumes have undergone less degassing
points.body: Comparing helium, neon, and argon isotopes between ocean ridge and plume basalts, plume samples consistently show lower radiogenic-to-primordial isotope ratios. Under this framework, this means the portion of mantle sampled by plumes has retained more primordial gas and has been less ‘processed’ by melting and plate tectonics—a relatively primitive reservoir that has not been thoroughly stirred.

points.h: Late veneer contributed more to the upper mantle's initial composition
points.body: Solar nebula gas, volatile-rich silicate materials (similar to carbonaceous chondrites), and comets each carry distinct neon isotope fingerprints from the three accretion sources. Using these fingerprints to reconstruct the initial mixing proportions of the two reservoirs, results show the upper mantle required a higher fraction of volatile-rich silicate material—consistent with the hypothesis that late veneer material, delivered after the Giant Impact forming the moon, preferentially mixed into the upper mantle.

points.h: Counterintuitively, mantle plume sources started poor in volatile gases
points.body: ‘Primitive’ does not mean ‘gas-rich.’ Plume sources have retained a larger proportion of initial gases, but this does not mean they were absolutely rich in gases—that depends on how much they started with. Forward modeling fitted simultaneously to today's helium, neon, and xenon isotope ratios reveals that ‘less degassing’ alone cannot explain the data; it also requires assuming that plume sources had lower initial gas concentrations than the upper mantle. The result unexpectedly shows that plume sources began volatile-poor.

points.h: Today's mantle plume sources contain roughly 20 times more water than the upper mantle
points.body: At the end of Earth's accretion, plume sources had 4 to 250 times less water than the upper mantle. This dry, rigid early mantle plume may have resisted mixing, perhaps explaining why the Giant Impact did not homogenize the early Earth, and might account for why plume sources retained more early isotopic heterogeneity. But today's plume sources contain roughly 400–1000 ppm water, actually wetter than ocean ridge sources' 50–200 ppm, indicating that most water in today's plumes is not primordial but was added later.

points.h: Subduction has delivered surface water deep into the mantle for only 2.5 billion years
points.body: Water reaches plume sources through subduction zones either when descending slabs carry hydrous minerals deeper than the magma generation zone, or when rising plumes pass through the transition zone and entrain water-rich material. Using the 15-year-accumulated record of ancient atmospheric xenon isotope evolution as a ‘fingerprint’ to work backward, researchers found that around 2.5 billion years ago, the mantle would have been unable to absorb such large quantities of atmospheric xenon without leaving an isotopic anomaly visible today—which we do not observe. This indicates that subduction zones became sufficiently cold to retain volatiles in the slab and transport them to depth only within the last 2.5 billion years, though it does not necessarily mean plate tectonics itself began then.

points.h: The upper mantle and plume sources have reversed their water balance over Earth's history
points.body: The upper mantle began relatively water-rich but has lost most of its original volatiles through melting and degassing over Earth's history, now maintaining rough equilibrium between degassing and atmospheric input. Plume sources show the opposite: initially dry, their current water content derives mostly from the surface—introduced through subduction zone cycling or entrainment as plumes rise through the transition zone—completely reversing the positions of the two reservoirs.

terms.def: A column of hot material rising vertically from deep within the mantle, driving hotspot volcanism (such as Hawaii).
An isotope present since Earth's accretion, not produced by internal nuclear reactions; used as a fingerprint for material origins.
An isotope continuously produced by the decay of radioactive elements such as uranium and thorium; used to measure degassing degree.
Material added to Earth after the Giant Impact that formed the moon, believed to have preferentially mixed into the upper mantle.

facts.k: Mantle plume source water relative to upper mantle at end of accretion

quotes.text: You also need for there to have been a difference in the initial gas concentration, with the plume mantle surprisingly being gas-poor compared to the upper mantle.
At the end of accretion, my calculation was that the plume source would have at least four times less water, up to 250 times less water than the upper mantle at the end of accretion.
So having a dry ancient plume mantle would be a dry, stiff ancient plume mantle. And that would be a reservoir that could resist mixing.
The amount of water in the plume source today, we think it's about 400 to 1000 parts per million H2O in the plume mantle. And that's wetter than the modern mid-ocean rich basalt source.
Yes, not recent in anyone's normal way of thinking about recent.
The upper mantle, I think, started relatively wet, and then over-Earth history lost most of its original gas through melting and outgassing.
